title: Mexico’s Archaeology Institute Reveals Findings in the Mundo Zoque Cave in Cintalapa, Chiapas
author: Alonso Urrutia and Arturo Sánchez
content:
_This article by Alonso Urrutia and Arturo Sánchez originally appeared in
the[August 21, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/08/21/cultura/inah-revela-
hallazgos-en-la-cueva-del-mundo-zoque-en-cintalapa-chiapas), Mexico’s premier
left-wing daily newspaper._

The director of the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH),
Omar Vázquez Herrera, announced a new archaeological find in the Chiapas
municipality of Cintalapa, where what is now called the Mundo Zoque Cave was
found.

> “A discovery we came upon from a report, where the INAH of course goes to
> the General Lázaro Cárdenas community in Cintalapa.”

Archaeologists recorded hundreds of pre-Hispanic pieces in the cave.

During the press conference at the National Palace — from which President
Claudia Sheinbaum was absent due to a cold — Vázquez reported that the find is
a cave 20 meters underground and 100 meters long. It was a pilgrimage site
where the Zoque people went to ask for rain and good harvests.

![INAH slide listing the cave's findings](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-21-mundo-zoque-cave-02-findings.jpg)Between
February and June, INAH recorded 13 offerings and 179 pre-Hispanic pieces in
the cave, dated to the Late Classic period (600–900 AD). Stalactites and
stalagmites were modified to resemble human figures or the jaws of the earth
monster. Photo: INAH

He specified that between January and June, 13 offerings and 179 pre-Hispanic
pieces have been located. The ceramic objects would have been made in the Late
Classic period, that is, between the years 600 and 900 of our era.

![INAH slide on the cave's iconography](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/2026-08-21-mundo-zoque-cave-03-iconography.jpg)Among
the iconography — jaguars, owls, and human figures — a standout piece is an
incense burner with a 32-cm handle bearing a quincunx, a figure alluding to
the four directions of the universe, on its bowl, and a serpent at the tip of
the handle. Photo: INAH

In addition to these pieces, stalactites and stalagmites modified to resemble
human figures or the jaws of a monster were found in the cave. Iconography
with figures of jaguars and owls was also found, along with an incense burner
with a 32-centimeter handle.

He said that studies will now be carried out to pinpoint the period in which
these pieces were made.

Vázquez said the find was made possible by the guide Jairo Díaz, who, after
locating the cave, informed the INAH of the site, to which the archaeologist
Josué Losada then traveled.

In a video released of the cave, Díaz explains that during that period
significant climatic changes were recorded that caused a lack of rain, which
is why the Zoque took refuge in this cave. He also explained that there are
still some Zoque communities today.
